newsitem.title: UK: Eurobourses lag Wall Street, dollar below highs.
newsitem.headline: Eurobourses lag Wall Street, dollar below highs.

text.p: European bourses rose on Monday, taking their cue from a rebound in New York, but nagging fears on interest rates and the outlook for Wall Street kept them from getting as enthusiastic as U.S. markets.
Dealers in London, Europe's biggest stock market, said many investors preferred to wait and see amid post-holiday torpor.

"There is still concern over interest rates. Gilts haven't done well today and European bonds also haven't had a good day. That has muted any positive impact from Wall Street," said Steve Wright, U.K. strategist at investment bank BZW.
After jumping 101.60 points on Friday, the Dow Jones industrial average added a further 66 points to 6,610 in morning trading in New York on growing optimism about the U.S. economy.
"The message from the stock market is perhaps the economy is stronger than anyone had bargained for," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany in New York.
Oil was fired up by fresh demand for heating oil in the United States. London February futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend rose 53 cents to $24.65 a barrel.

But on the bullion market, gold, which has been shunned by investors as stock markets hit record levels and low inflation detracted from its status as a "safe haven", slipped to its lowest since October 1993.

The dollar, meanwhile, was knocked off its strongest level against the yen since March 1993 after Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said Japan would "continue to deal appropriately" with extreme currency market movements.
The U.S. currency, which flirted with 117 yen in Asian trading, then hit a 115.40 low in European business, below late rates last week, before recovering some of its poise.
Dealers said Ogawa's comments took the market by surprise, with thin trading conditions exaggerating the reaction.
But analysts said negative perceptions of the Japanese economy and low interest rates there still prompted concern over an outflow of funds and should continue to bolster the dollar.
Tokyo markets made a shaky start to the new year on Monday as the yen slid to its lowest level against the dollar in almost four years, dragging stocks and bonds down in its wake.
The 225-share Nikkei average fell by as much as 150 points before reviving to close at 19,446.00, up 84.65 points.

Against the mark, the U.S. currency slipped from a high in Asian trading of 1.5714 but, at around 1.5665 marks, it was still above Friday's late European levels. Wall Street's gains also helped the dollar recover from its lows.

The pound sterling hit its highest level against the mark in more than four years before subsiding. It stood at 2.6425 marks, compared with an early high of 2.6615, its peak since crashing out of the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.
On the London stock market, Europe's busiest, shares were firmer after Wall Street's revival but fear of higher U.S. and British interest rates held them back.

"After the Dow's 100-point jump last Friday, a mark-up in London was inevitable but some players are worried about the Dow's volatility," a London dealer said. "The market knows the Dow could just as easily drop 100 points in a day, especially if we get any data which hints at higher rates.
German shares made a positive start to the week, gaining around one percent amid interest in blue-chip auto companies and as Wall Street built on its gains.

Shares in Paris also closed on a strong note, boosted by Wall Street's progress, strength in the dollar and hopes for more French interest rate cuts. But traders said recent sharp swings on the Dow in New York encouraged caution.

This week the main focus for markets will be U.S. jobs figures on Friday. If non-farm payroll statistics are stronger than forecast, raising fears of an overheating economy and higher inflation, jitters over higher rates could send stock and bond markets lower on both sides of the Atlantic, dealers said.
The dollar is also highly sensitive to moves in U.S. stock and bond markets, they noted.
German November manufacturing orders, December unemployment and December cost of living numbers are also due in coming days.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted around 1.5665 marks and 115.74 yen in late European trade, compared with 1.5580 and 116.33 on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The FTSE 100 index of key British shares ended 17.0 points higher at 4,106.5, 12 below its record close hit last week.
The 30-share DAX in Frankfurt closed floor trade 22.04 points up at 2,881.32 and rose to 2,890.20 in later electronic trading. In Paris, the CAC-40 index was up 23.91 at 2,306.67.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold weakened on fresh speculative selling to end London trading at $357.95 an ounce, down $4.20, after an afternoon fix of $358.50. Silver slipped two cents to $4.67.
